To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Spanish crisis was not the result of a current account deficit and a large net foreign debt but rather of an excessive amount of bank debt and a huge volume of gross external debt that was not matched by a large volume of gross external assets.

gross external debt was the key variable that drove capital flows in Spain during the Great Financial Crisis and that the residence of debt-holders is relevant for the analysis of the crisis in Spain and the Euro Zone.

Spain’s current account deficit was a secondary driver of gross external liabilities, and that the primary cause of Spain’s gross external liabilities was the large volume of bank debt that banks refinanced with the help of international markets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following issues: 1. What is the relationship between current account imbalances and gross capital inflows?
the question of whether the current account deficit is the main driver of the gross external debt or whether bank credit is.
the question of whether current account imbalances or too much bank debt was the main driver of gross capital inflows in the Spanish economy during the Great Financial Crisis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the main driver of Spain’s external imbalances was bank credit and that Spain was not at the epicenter, but rather at the periphery of the crisis.

the crisis in the euro zone was the result of a huge accumulation of bank debt in the private sector, which was financed in international markets and was not matched by a similar increase in foreign direct investment, which would have been the best option for the country’s external exposure.
the crisis in the euro zone was caused by the excessive credit expansion in the banking system and the lack of adequate regulation and supervision.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the main problem in Spain was not the large accumulated current account deficit but the excessive amount of bank debt, which was financed by international markets.
the Spanish case shows that the current account imbalances are the result of the bank debt and not vice versa.
the main problem in the Euro Zone is the huge volume of credit that banks have refinanced in international financial markets and the huge volume of external debt accumulated as the result.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a country’s external exposure is a function of the volume of credit that its banks extend, not of the size of current account deficits.

the principle cause of the Euro Zone crisis was not the accumulation of current account deficits and external debt, but rather the excessive credit expansion in the banking system, with the accumulation of current accounts deficits playing a secondary role.

a focus on net external debt and current account deficits, as the main driver of gross external liabilities, is misleading and that a more accurate analysis of international financial flows is required.
